title: skills for driving trucks and trailers

cards.front: When you start backing up a tractor with a semi-trailer, which way do you turn the steering wheel?
cards.back: Turn the steering wheel in the direction OPPOSITE to where you want the trailer to go. As soon as the trailer begins to turn, turn the wheel the other way — in the same direction the trailer is travelling — so the tractor follows a path that matches the trailer's path.

cards.front: When towing two trailers, which trailer should be coupled to the tractor?
cards.back: Couple the more heavily loaded trailer to the tractor, with the lighter trailer behind. Different trailer weights affect the handling of the combination. Note the last trailer in a combination is the most likely to roll over.

cards.front: List causes of trailer whipping and swerving.
cards.back: Driving too fast for the conditions, sudden steering changes, improper trailer connections, shifting loads, dragging brakes, or a flat tire.

cards.front: What should you do if your trailer whips or swerves?
cards.back: Slow down and stop as soon as it's safe, then check your vehicle and load. Even if the swerving stops when you slow down, stopping to check is still important — the whipping may have shifted your cargo or loosened a trailer connection.

cards.front: Why must you block the wheels of a parked trailer that has no spring brakes?
cards.back: The air in the trailer air tank bleeds down over time. Without spring brakes, the trailer brakes will release as air pressure drops, so the trailer could roll if the wheels aren't blocked.

cards.front: How do you check that the fifth wheel has properly connected to the trailer kingpin?
cards.back: Check that the fifth wheel jaws have engaged the kingpin, there's no space or daylight between the fifth wheel and the trailer apron, and the release handle is in the locked position. Go under the trailer with a flashlight to check the locking jaws are securely closed around the kingpin (remove the ignition keys first).

cards.front: When uncoupling, how do you ease the pressure on the fifth wheel locking jaws?
cards.back: Set the trailer brakes, release the tractor brakes, back up gently, and apply the tractor parking brakes while the tractor is pushing against the trailer. The tractor may only move a few centimetres, but this eases pressure on the locking jaws.

cards.front: What extra securing devices are required when you use any coupling device other than a fifth wheel?
cards.back: Chains or metal cables connecting the towed and towing vehicles. These auxiliary chains or cables must be equal to the strength of the coupling device.

cards.front: What is the maximum length of the drawbar or other connection between a motor vehicle and a trailer?
cards.back: No more than five metres long, unless you're towing a pole trailer.

cards.front: What is a converter dolly?
cards.back: A device sometimes used when towing more than one trailer. It has an axle, a fifth wheel and a hitch. When towing with one, make sure the air brake lines from truck to dolly and dolly to trailer are properly connected so the trailer brakes function.

cards.front: How should cargo weight be distributed on a trailer (tractor-trailer combination)?
cards.back: Approximately 45 per cent of the cargo weight on the trailer axle unit, 45 per cent on the drive axle unit and 10 per cent on the steering axle. Place cargo midway between the rear axle unit and the drive axle unit.

cards.front: What forces must a cargo securement system be able to withstand?
cards.back: 0.8g deceleration in a forward direction, 0.5g deceleration rearward, 0.5g acceleration in either sideways direction, and a downward force equal to at least 20 per cent of the cargo weight.

cards.front: What is the rough guide for the number of tiedowns on a load?
cards.back: Use two tiedowns for the first 3.04 m of a load and one tiedown for every 3.04 m after that. Consider the length of the cargo first and then its weight. If cargo is prevented from moving forward, the minimum is one tiedown for every 3.04 m of length.

cards.front: What is the minimum required strength of tiedowns securing cargo?
cards.back: The aggregate working load limit of the tiedowns must be at least 50 per cent of the cargo weight. For example, for a 600 kg article the tiedowns' combined working load limit must be no less than 300 kg.

cards.front: What is dunnage?
cards.back: Spacing blocks, boards and mats that separate cargo from itself and its restraints — for example, corner boards used with tiedowns. Timber used as dunnage, chocks or cradles must be strong enough not to be split or crushed by the cargo or tiedowns.

cards.front: What are the height and strength requirements for a front-end structure?
cards.back: It must be no shorter than 122 cm above the deck (or the height at which it prevents cargo moving forward). If less than 1.83 m tall it must withstand a static load of at least 50 per cent of total cargo weight; if 1.83 m or taller, 40 per cent. It must resist penetration at a deceleration of 6.1 m/s².

cards.front: What are the limits for front and rear load projections?
cards.back: Front: no more than one metre beyond the front wheels (or front bumper if equipped). Rear (straight truck): no more than four metres beyond the turn centre. A load projecting more than 1.2 m beyond the rear needs a red flag or cloth in daylight, or a red light at night.

cards.front: What are the maximum legal height and width of a commercial vehicle and its load?
cards.back: Maximum height 4.15 m and maximum width 2.6 m, unless the driver has an oversize load permit. Vehicles carrying loose hay, straw or fodder may be loaded to a maximum 3.1 m overall width.

cards.front: Why are liquid or dry bulk tank loads and hanging meat especially dangerous?
cards.back: They have a high centre of gravity, which increases the danger of rollover. Unbaffled liquid loads surge forward, backward and side to side; suspended meat can sway. Reduce speed on curves, sharp turns, ramps, and be careful on stops and starts.

cards.front: What precautions apply when transporting livestock?
cards.back: Animals may move around, making turns difficult and possibly causing a collision. With less than a full load, use false bulkheads to keep livestock bunched together. Reduce speed on curves — even bunched animals sometimes lean, shifting the centre of gravity and possibly causing a rollover.

cards.front: How far must a pilot car travel from the oversize vehicle it's escorting?
cards.back: Between 100 and 500 m, either behind or in front of the oversize vehicle. A pilot car warns other drivers about the larger-than-normal vehicle, and when required must carry a D (over dimension) sign.

cards.front: Who must report to a weigh scale in B.C.?
cards.back: Drivers of commercial vehicles with a licensed gross vehicle weight of more than 5,500 kg must report to a scale whenever a sign, a police officer or an authorized person directs them to. The vehicle is weighed and inspected. Scales are fixed (permanent, marked by highway signs) or portable (set up by travelling inspectors on any public road).

cards.front: Where must shipping documents be when you transport dangerous goods?
cards.back: All shipping documents must be complete, correct and readily available in the cab, and must accompany the dangerous goods shipment.

cards.front: What must you do if there's an incident involving your dangerous goods cargo (spill, leak, fire, explosion or damaged container)?
cards.back: Report it immediately to the nearest police agency or the Provincial Emergency Program (1-800-663-3456 in B.C.). Rapid action may help prevent an incident from becoming serious.

cards.front: Name the nine classes of dangerous goods.
cards.back: Explosives; gases; flammable liquids; flammable solids; oxidizing substances and organic peroxides; poisonous (toxic) substances and infectious substances; radioactive materials; corrosive substances; and miscellaneous products or substances.

cards.front: Where do dangerous goods placards appear on transport trucks?
cards.back: On the sides and both ends of the truck. Each placard identifies the class of dangerous goods being carried (there's also a placard for a mixed load).

cards.front: What training and certification is required to work with dangerous goods?
cards.back: You must be properly trained and appropriately certified. Your current employer must certify that you've had appropriate training, and you must always carry your training certificate with you when transporting dangerous goods.

cards.front: What do dangerous goods route signs indicate?
cards.back: One sign designates roads where vehicles transporting dangerous goods may travel; another designates roads where these vehicles can't travel.

questions.q: When you first start backing up a tractor with a semi-trailer, you should turn the steering wheel:
choices: in the same direction you want the trailer to go
as little as possible until the trailer straightens
in the direction opposite to where you want the trailer to go
fully to the left, regardless of trailer direction
questions.explanation: Turn the wheel opposite to the direction you want the trailer to go when you start backing up. Once the trailer begins to turn, turn the wheel the other way to follow the trailer's path.

questions.q: When backing up, what can cause your tractor-trailer to jackknife?
choices: Backing up with the trailer brakes released
The tractor failing to follow a path that matches the trailer's path
Using the lowest reverse gear
Backing up in a perfectly straight line
questions.explanation: As the trailer begins to turn, the tractor must follow a path that matches the trailer's path — if it doesn't, you risk jackknifing.

questions.q: When towing two trailers of different weights, how should they be arranged?
choices: The lighter trailer coupled to the tractor, heavier behind
Order doesn't matter if both are within legal weight
The longer trailer always behind, regardless of weight
The more heavily loaded trailer coupled to the tractor, lighter behind
questions.explanation: Couple the more heavily loaded trailer to the tractor with the lighter trailer behind, since trailer weights affect the handling of the combination.

questions.q: Why should you never unlock the pintle hook while the dolly is still under the rear trailer?
choices: The dolly tow bar may fly up, possibly causing injury, and make re-coupling very difficult
The trailer air tanks will immediately drain
The rear trailer's spring brakes will release
The fifth wheel jaws will be damaged
questions.explanation: With the dolly still under the rear trailer, unlocking the pintle hook can let the tow bar fly up, possibly causing injury and making it very difficult to re-couple.

questions.q: Your trailer begins to whip and swerve. What should you do?
choices: Speed up slightly to pull the trailer straight
Apply the trailer hand valve fully and continue
Slow down and stop as soon as it's safe, then check your vehicle and load
Ignore it if it stops when you change lanes
questions.explanation: Slow down and stop as soon as it's safe. Even if the swerving stops when you slow down, stop and check — it may have shifted your cargo or loosened a trailer connection.

questions.q: During fifth wheel coupling, when should you stop the first time you back up toward the trailer?
choices: When the kingpin locks into the fifth wheel jaws
When the rear tractor tires touch the landing gear
About one metre before reaching the trailer
When the fifth wheel just touches the trailer apron
questions.explanation: Back up slowly and stop when the fifth wheel just touches the trailer apron — don't back up too far, and back in a straight line, not at an angle.

questions.q: How is the tug test performed after coupling with a fifth wheel?
choices: Apply full throttle in a forward gear to try to break away
Rock the trailer sideways using the steering
Release the tractor brakes with the trailer brakes still applied, and gently tug against them
Release all brakes and roll forward 10 metres
questions.explanation: With the landing gear slightly off the ground, release the tractor brakes (trailer brakes still applied) and gently tug — the trailer brakes should prevent the trailer from moving.

questions.q: When uncoupling a tractor from a semi-trailer, when are the air lines disconnected?
choices: After the tractor has completely pulled away
Before pulling the fifth wheel release handle to unlock the jaws
While the tractor is moving slowly forward
Only after the landing gear is fully raised
questions.explanation: In the uncoupling sequence, you block the wheels, lower the landing gear, disconnect the air lines and electrical cable and secure them to the tractor, and then pull the fifth wheel release handle.

questions.q: When a coupling device other than a fifth wheel is used, what else is required to connect the vehicles?
choices: Chains or metal cables equal to the strength of the coupling device
A converter dolly between the two vehicles
A second pintle hook as backup
Nothing else, if the pintle hook has a safety latch
questions.explanation: With any coupling device other than a fifth wheel, you must also use auxiliary chains or metal cables equal to the strength of the coupling device.

questions.q: Except for pole trailers, what is the maximum permitted length for the drawbar or connection between a motor vehicle and trailer?
choices: 2.25 metres
3.04 metres
Five metres
Ten metres
questions.explanation: The drawbar or other connection may not be more than five metres long unless you're towing a pole trailer.

questions.q: Five-ton freight trucks are designed to carry approximately what share of cargo weight on the rear axle(s)?
choices: 90 per cent, with 10 per cent on the steering axle
45 per cent, with 55 per cent on the steering axle
70 per cent, with 30 per cent on the steering axle
50 per cent, with 50 per cent on the steering axle
questions.explanation: Five-ton freight trucks are designed for about 90 per cent of cargo weight on the rear axle(s) and 10 per cent on the steering axle; cement mixers and dump trucks are designed for about 70/30.

questions.q: When loaded, a tridem drive truck or truck tractor must have a combined steering axle weight of at least:
choices: 10 per cent of the tridem axle weight
50 per cent of the gross vehicle weight
70 per cent of the tridem axle weight
25 per cent of the tridem axle weight (40 per cent for twin steering axles)
questions.explanation: A tridem drive truck or tractor requires a loaded steering axle weight of at least 25 per cent of the tridem axle weight — 40 per cent in the case of twin steering axles.

questions.q: A cargo securement system must be able to withstand what deceleration in the forward direction?
questions.explanation: The system must withstand 0.8g deceleration forward, 0.5g rearward, 0.5g sideways in either direction, and a downward force of at least 20 per cent of the cargo weight.

questions.q: An article of cargo is 1.21 m long, weighs 600 kg, and is not prevented from moving forward. What is the minimum number of tiedowns?
choices: Two, equally spaced
One
Four
Three, equally spaced
questions.explanation: Articles 1.52 m or shorter but over 500 kg require a minimum of two tiedowns when not prevented from moving forward.

questions.q: A 3.65 m article weighing 600 kg needs three tiedowns. What minimum working load limit must each tiedown have?
choices: 600 kg each
50 kg each
100 kg each
300 kg each
questions.explanation: The aggregate working load limit must be at least 50 per cent of cargo weight (300 kg for a 600 kg article), so each of the three tiedowns must be rated at not less than 100 kg.

questions.q: A friction mat not marked by the manufacturer with a working load limit is assumed to provide resistance to horizontal movement equal to:
choices: 50 per cent of the weight of the cargo resting on the mat
100 per cent of the cargo weight
20 per cent of the cargo weight
Nothing — unmarked mats can't be used
questions.explanation: An unmarked friction mat is assumed to provide resistance equal to 50 per cent of the weight of the cargo resting on it.

questions.q: Which of the following may NOT be used as an anchor point for tiedowns?
choices: The vehicle frame
Rub rails
The body rail
Purpose-built anchor points inboard of the rub rail
questions.explanation: Rub rails must not be used as anchor points. Tiedowns should be located inboard of rub rails if possible.

questions.q: When must an aggregate load (such as sand, gravel or wood chips) be covered with a tarp?
choices: Only when it weighs more than 2,268 kg
Only when travelling on a highway at night
Never — sideboards are always sufficient
When the load can't be contained with sideboards or tiedowns and is likely to bounce, blow or drop from the moving vehicle
questions.explanation: You must use a cover or tarp if the load is made up of aggregate material and is likely to bounce, blow or drop from the moving vehicle.

questions.q: A front-end structure less than 1.83 m in height must be able to withstand a static load of at least:
choices: 20 per cent of the total cargo weight
50 per cent of the total cargo weight, uniformly distributed
40 per cent of the total cargo weight
100 per cent of the total cargo weight
questions.explanation: Front-end structures under 1.83 m must withstand at least 50 per cent of total cargo weight; structures 1.83 m or taller must withstand 40 per cent.

questions.q: To protect the vehicle operator, a front-end structure must be no shorter than what height above the deck?
choices: 183 cm
100 cm
152 cm
122 cm (or the height at which it prevents the cargo from moving forward)
questions.explanation: The Standard requires a front-end structure no shorter than 122 cm above the deck, or the height at which it prevents the cargo from moving forward.

questions.q: A load projects more than 1.2 m beyond the rear of your vehicle. What must be attached to the tip of the projection?
choices: An orange triangle at all times
A red flag or cloth in daylight, or a red light at night
A white flag in daylight, or an amber light at night
Nothing, if the projection is under four metres
questions.explanation: If a load projects more than 1.2 m beyond the rear, attach a red flag or cloth for daylight driving, or a red light at night. Loads on a straight truck can't extend more than four metres beyond the turn centre.

questions.q: The Standard's specific requirements for coils of rolled sheet metal apply when the shipment of coils weighs:
choices: 500 kg or more
5,000 kg or more
2,268 kg or more
4,500 kg or more
questions.explanation: The Standard outlines specific requirements for transporting coils of rolled sheet metal where the shipment weighs 2,268 kg or more (the same threshold applies to paper roll shipments).

questions.q: A heavy vehicle weighing more than 4,500 kg carried as cargo must be restrained by:
choices: A minimum of four tiedowns, each with a working load limit of at least 2,268 kg
Two tiedowns at the rear only
One chain at each corner rated at 500 kg
Synthetic webbing straps at the front and rear
questions.explanation: Heavy vehicles over 4,500 kg need at least four tiedowns, each with a working load limit of at least 2,268 kg; vehicles under 4,500 kg GVW need a minimum of two tiedowns securing front and rear.

questions.q: Which two types of loads have a high centre of gravity that increases the chance of rollover if movement or swaying isn't prevented?
choices: Dressed lumber and concrete pipe
Intermodal containers and boulders
Crushed vehicles and building products
Hanging meat and liquid bulk tank loads
questions.explanation: Meat suspended in a trailer can sway and liquid bulk loads surge; both have a high centre of gravity, increasing the danger of rollover — reduce speed on curves and ramps.

questions.q: What is the maximum allowable height for a commercial vehicle without an oversize load permit?
questions.explanation: The maximum allowable height is 4.15 m unless the driver has an oversize load permit. The maximum legal width of vehicle and load is 2.6 m.

questions.q: Oversize permits are not normally given for loads or vehicles wider than:
questions.explanation: Permits are not normally given for loads or vehicles wider than 4.4 m. Oversize extremities must be marked with red flags at least 30 cm by 30 cm, with amber lights to the front and red to the rear at night.

questions.q: A pilot car escorting an oversize vehicle must travel:
choices: Directly beside the oversize vehicle
At least one kilometre ahead
Within 50 m of the oversize vehicle at all times
Between 100 and 500 m either behind or in front of the oversize vehicle
questions.explanation: A pilot car must travel between 100 and 500 m either behind or in front of the oversize vehicle it's escorting, warning other drivers about the larger-than-normal vehicle.

questions.q: Which drivers must report to a weigh scale when directed by a sign, police officer or authorized person?
choices: Only drivers carrying dangerous goods
Drivers of commercial vehicles with a licensed GVW of more than 5,500 kg
All drivers of any vehicle towing a trailer
Only drivers of vehicles over 4,500 kg net weight
questions.explanation: If you drive a commercial vehicle with a licensed gross vehicle weight of more than 5,500 kg, you must report to a scale whenever a sign, police officer or authorized person directs you to.

questions.q: How might you encounter a portable weigh scale in B.C.?
choices: Only at permanent scale yards marked by highway signs
Only at border crossings
Set up temporarily at the roadside, or a vehicle with flashing lights may pull you over and the inspector sets up a scale
Only on designated truck routes within city limits
questions.explanation: Portable scales may be temporarily set up on the side of a road where you'll be signalled to stop, or a vehicle with flashing lights may direct you to pull over and the inspector may then set up a scale.

questions.q: How many classes of dangerous goods are there?
choices: Six
Nine
Twelve
Four
questions.explanation: There are nine classes: explosives, gases, flammable liquids, flammable solids, oxidizing substances and organic peroxides, poisonous and infectious substances, radioactive materials, corrosive substances, and miscellaneous products or substances.

questions.q: When transporting dangerous goods, where must the shipping documents be?
choices: Filed at the carrier's head office
Mailed ahead to the destination
Locked in the trailer with the cargo
Complete, correct and readily available in the cab
questions.explanation: You must ensure all shipping documents are complete, correct and readily available in the cab, and they must accompany the dangerous goods shipment.

questions.q: You discover a leak in your dangerous goods cargo. What must you do?
choices: Report it immediately to the nearest police agency or the Provincial Emergency Program
Note it in your log book and report it at the end of the trip
Continue to the nearest weigh scale for inspection
Report it only if the leak causes a fire
questions.explanation: Report immediately any incident related to dangerous goods cargo — spills, leaks, fires, explosions or damaged containers — to the nearest police agency or the Provincial Emergency Program (1-800-663-3456).

questions.q: Where do dangerous goods placards appear on a transport truck?
choices: Only on the rear doors
Only in the cab window
On the sides and both ends of the truck
On the roof of the trailer
questions.explanation: Dangerous goods placards may appear on the sides and both ends of transport trucks, identifying the class of dangerous goods carried.

questions.q: What must you always carry with you when transporting dangerous goods?
choices: A letter from a professional engineer
A copy of the Commercial Transport Regulations
An oversize load permit
Your dangerous goods training certificate
questions.explanation: Your current employer must certify that you've had appropriate training, and you must always carry your training certificate with you when transporting dangerous goods.

questions.q: Who must certify that a driver has had appropriate dangerous goods training?
choices: The driver's current employer
ICBC
The local police department
The Provincial Emergency Program
questions.explanation: If you're going to work with dangerous goods, your current employer must certify that you've had appropriate training.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the nine classes of dangerous goods?
choices: Perishable foodstuffs
Aggregate materials
Corrosive substances
Livestock
questions.explanation: Corrosive substances is one of the nine classes. Perishable foods, aggregates and livestock are not dangerous goods classes.

questions.q: What do the dangerous goods route signs described in the manual indicate?
choices: The speed limit for placarded vehicles
Roads where vehicles transporting dangerous goods may travel, and roads where they can't
Locations of emergency response depots
Mandatory rest stops for dangerous goods drivers
questions.explanation: One sign designates roads where vehicles transporting dangerous goods may travel; the other designates roads where these vehicles can't travel.
